title: Malted Oats Versus Flaked Oats | Craft Beer School
desc: Malted oats or flaked oats? What each adds to body, haze and flavour, how much to use, mashing tips and using supermarket oats in India.
teaser: Oats make beer silky. Which kind of oat you use decides whether you get silk, nuttiness or a stuck mash.
standfirst: Oats are behind the smooth body of oatmeal stouts and hazy IPAs. Brewers can buy them flaked or malted. The two behave quite differently. Here is how to choose.
sections: Why brewers use oats at all

Oats are rich in beta-glucans, protein and some oil. Beta-glucans are gummy carbohydrates that thicken liquid, which is why porridge sets. In beer, they add body and a soft, silky mouthfeel. Oat proteins help create haze and can support foam.

Those same properties cause trouble in the brewhouse. Too many beta-glucans make the mash sticky and the runoff slow. Getting the benefits without the mess is a question of which oats you use and how much.
Flaked oats: raw, rolled and ready to mash

Flaked oats are whole oat groats that have been steamed and rolled flat. The steaming gelatinises the starch, so flakes can go straight into the mash without cooking. They are raw grain: no germination, no enzymes and no breakdown of beta-glucans.

That makes flaked oats the most powerful choice for body and haze. They give a creamy, slightly grainy character with little flavour of their own. Most of the silky texture in a hazy IPA or oatmeal stout comes from flakes. Because they have no husk and plenty of beta-glucan, they also make lautering harder at high rates.

Malted oats have been steeped, germinated and kilned like barley malt. During germination, the grain's own enzymes break down much of the beta-glucan and protein. Kilning adds flavour.

The result is an oat that gives a gentler body boost than flakes, with a pleasant nutty or biscuity flavour. Malted oats usually keep their husk, which helps the grain bed filter during lautering. Some malted oats carry useful enzyme activity, although less than barley malt. Some speciality oat malts are kilned or stewed to give a crystal-like, toasty character. Check the maltster's specification to see which kind you have.

Starting points for common styles:

  • Oatmeal stout: 5 to 10% flaked oats for smoothness. Many brewers add a little malted oat for flavour.
  • Hazy or New England IPA: 10 to 20% flaked oats, sometimes with wheat.
  • Pale ale or session beer: 5 to 10% malted oats for a touch of body and a nutty note.
  • Oat beers such as a Dutch kuit: high oat shares, which need careful mash handling.

Above about 20% oats, expect slow runoffs unless you take precautions. Our guide to oats in beer covers the styles in more depth.
Mashing tips for high oat grists

Three habits keep an oat mash moving:

  • Add rice hulls. About 2 to 5% of the grist weight gives the grain bed a filter structure that oat flakes lack.
  • Consider a beta-glucan rest. A short rest around 40 to 45 °C lets glucanase enzymes in the malt break down some gum before the main mash. Many modern malts make this optional, but it helps at high oat rates.
  • Keep the mash warm at sparge. Mashing out at about 76 °C thins the wort and speeds runoff.

The one floor detail that warns you early: watch the pressure difference across the grain bed, or on a homebrew system, how fast the first runnings slow. If the flow halves in the first ten minutes, stop and stir rather than pulling harder on the pump. Our guide to beta-glucan problems with oats explains the chemistry.

The haze in an oat-heavy beer comes largely from proteins binding with polyphenols from malt and hops. That haze is intended in a hazy IPA. In an oatmeal stout nobody can see it, but in a pale session beer it may not be what you want. If clarity matters, keep oats at the lower end of the range and give the beer time cold before packaging.

Oats also carry more oil than barley. Oil and fatty acids can work against foam and, over time, contribute to stale, cardboard-like flavours as they oxidise. Fresh oats, low oxygen pickup at packaging and cold storage all help. That matters more in India than in cooler countries, because a beer that sits in a warm godown or a shop shelf ages faster.

None of this is a reason to avoid oats. It is a reason to drink oat beers fresh and to brew them in batch sizes you can sell quickly.

Brewer's flaked oats can be hard to buy in small quantities in India. Plain rolled oats from a supermarket are a reasonable stand-in. They are steamed and rolled in much the same way. Quick-cooking or instant oats are rolled thinner and cut smaller. They work too but can make the mash stickier.

Check the pack carefully. Avoid anything with added sugar, salt, milk powder, flavouring or masala. Plain oats only. Buy a fresh pack, because oat oils go rancid in heat. A pack that smells stale or like old paint will make the beer taste that way.

Malted oats are a specialist product and usually need to be bought from a malt importer or homebrew supplier.

If you want maximum body and haze, use flaked oats. If you want flavour and an easier brew day, use malted oats. Many good recipes use both. Understanding why the two behave so differently, through beta-glucans, enzymes and protein, is the kind of grain chemistry that makes recipe design predictable rather than lucky.

Your first step: brew your next pale ale with 8% flaked oats in place of the same weight of base malt, then compare its body with your usual version.
faqs: What is the difference between malted and flaked oats?
Flaked oats are raw oats steamed and rolled, with no enzymes and lots of beta-glucan. Malted oats are germinated and kilned, so they are gentler on body and add a nutty flavour.
Can I use supermarket oats in beer?
Yes, plain rolled oats work. Avoid any with added sugar, salt or flavour. Buy a fresh pack so the oils are not stale.
How do I stop oats causing a stuck mash?
Add 2 to 5% rice hulls, consider a short rest around 40 to 45 °C and mash out at about 76 °C to thin the wort.
